entities.name: Facundus of Hermiane
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Facundus of Hermiane, a steadfast 6th-century Christian author and bishop from the Roman province of Byzacena in North Africa, stands as a pivotal figure in the tumultuous Three Chapters Controversy. Dying around 570 CE, his unwavering theological opposition to Emperor Justinian I's condemnation of the 'Three Chapters'—a set of writings by Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Ibas of Edessa—made him a leading voice for ecclesiastical independence against imperial theological imposition. His principled defiance during a period of intense imperial-papal struggle profoundly shaped the discourse on religious authority in the Byzantine world and beyond.

His primary contribution was the monumental ten-book treatise, *Pro defensione Trium Capitulorum* (In Defense of the Three Chapters), composed between 547 and 550 CE. This work meticulously argued that condemning these figures posthumously undermined the Council of Chalcedon's authority and was an unjust capitulation to Monophysite demands. Facundus presented this defense directly to Emperor Justinian I in Constantinople, advocating passionately against the imperial edict. His refusal to conform, even as Pope Vigilius initially capitulated under duress at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553 CE, led to his extended exile and the severance of communion with the imperial church, particularly after Vigilius's eventual endorsement of the condemnation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Facundus's unwavering theological defense against imperial pressure preserved a critical perspective within the Three Chapters Controversy, directly influencing a major schism that lasted for decades in the Western Church. His writings remain a vital source for understanding 6th-century ecclesiastical politics and the struggle for doctrinal autonomy.
